Closing an RESP: follow contributions, returned benefits and accumulated income separately

Four original charts separate a hypothetical contribution refund, government-benefit repayment and accumulated income payment, then compare current cash with an eligible retirement-plan deduction.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Separate an RESP balance into contribution refunds, returned benefits, and taxable accumulated income

Interactive planning lab

Maximum modeled qualifying AIP deduction$10,000
Subscriber cash after illustrative final tax$40,000
Illustrative regular and additional AIP tax$8,000

Original hypothetical closeout ledger reviewed against CRA public guidance on 25 October 2026. Assume the RESP contract and promoter permit a valid AIP to one original subscriber who meets all current CRA payment conditions; the subscriber is resident in Canada. The specific beneficiary, age and plan-history eligibility checks have already been confirmed outside this model. Subscriber contributions and government/provincial benefits shown have been confirmed payable/refundable or repayable by the promoter. Only contribution refund, benefit repayment and eligible AIP balances enter the snapshot. The modeled subscriber qualifies for the AIP-related lifetime tax reduction; its remaining CAD 50,000 lifetime limit, actual available tax-year deduction capacity and AIP amount each cap the comparison. The entered regular rate is an illustrative flat incremental assumption, not an actual tax bracket, return, advice or prediction. Additional tax is 20% outside Quebec; Quebec’s 12% rate is excluded. All scenario amounts and individual tax components are rounded to cents. The result compares no qualifying deduction with the maximum amount supported by the inputs; it does not verify eligibility, RRSP room, contribution timing, promoter terms, withholding, final tax or future RRSP withdrawal tax. No cash-payment date, benefit eligibility, inflation, investment return, fees or school/EAP scenario is modeled. The first AIP requires RESP termination by the end of February in the following year. This model neither schedules that deadline nor calculates other termination or provincial rules.

The central idea

A remaining RESP balance can contain amounts with different destinations and taxes. Apply an AIP deduction only after the payment, taxpayer, lifetime ceiling and actual deduction capacity qualify.

01

Give every remaining dollar a payment type

An RESP statement balance does not identify how much is subscriber contribution, government benefit or accumulated investment income. Those amounts can have different destinations when an education plan is wound down. Build a dated component ledger only after the promoter confirms the applicable balances and permitted payments.

The illustration starts with CAD 32,000 of refundable subscriber contributions, CAD 6,400 of government benefits to repay, and a separately confirmed CAD 26,000 accumulated income payment (AIP). They sum to CAD 64,400. These numbers are invented; they do not estimate any person’s plan or grant recovery.

The federal RESP closeout overview describes returning personal contributions without tax, returning grant benefits to government, and options for accumulated interest. CRA’s RESP payment guide distinguishes a contribution refund, education assistance payment, AIP, repayment and transfer. The bars retain that distinction rather than calling the total balance a tax-free withdrawal.

The inputs already assume that the promoter has established the benefit-repayment amount and the AIP that can be paid. A grant percentage cannot be applied to the total plan balance to infer a repayment. Contributions may previously have been withdrawn, beneficiaries and provincial benefits may affect the result, and the relevant records matter.

02

Confirm the AIP payment conditions before estimating tax

An AIP is the plan’s accumulated income paid to or for a subscriber; it excludes contribution refunds, education assistance payments, repayments and certain transfers. The model assumes the plan contract and promoter permit a valid AIP for one qualifying Canadian-resident original subscriber.

Under CRA’s 2026 RESP guide, a payment must be for a Canadian-resident subscriber and only one subscriber. In the selected eligibility route, the plan has passed the year of its ninth anniversary and each living person who is or was a beneficiary is at least 21 and no longer eligible for an education assistance payment. Other routes and special cases exist. The charting tool does not decide whether a real plan satisfies any of them.

The CRA guide says an RESP must be terminated by the end of February in the year after its first AIP. The government closeout overview also advises checking the plan promoter’s terms. This page maps the amount only; it does not schedule an application, payout or termination.

Eligibility to receive an AIP, eligibility to deduct an RRSP contribution and the amount available under a lifetime AIP tax limit are different checks. The example assumes each has been verified separately. A valid general tax calculation cannot make an unpermitted payment eligible.

03

Apply a qualifying deduction to the remaining AIP tax bases

CRA describes AIPs as subject to regular income tax and a separate additional tax. The additional rate is 20% outside Quebec and 12% for a Quebec resident. A subscriber who meets the applicable requirements can reduce the AIP amount subject to these taxes by contributing to an RRSP, pooled registered pension plan (PRPP) or specified pension plan (SPP), or certain spouse plans, and claiming a deduction within the available limit.

The reduction is subject to a CAD 50,000 lifetime maximum across qualifying AIP relief, the eligible contribution amount, the deduction capacity and its timing. The CRA payment guide says the contribution must be made in the receipt year or the first 60 days of the following year, with sufficient deduction limit and the deduction claimed for the applicable year. Past use of the AIP lifetime limit is separate from available RRSP room.

For a transparent example, suppose the subscriber has CAD 15,000 of verified deduction capacity and has already used CAD 40,000 of the CAD 50,000 lifetime AIP relief limit. The most this scenario can model is CAD 10,000: the lesser of the CAD 26,000 AIP, the CAD 15,000 available capacity and the remaining CAD 10,000 lifetime ceiling.

At the selected hypothetical 30% regular incremental rate, taking no qualifying deduction leaves CAD 26,000 exposed to an illustrative CAD 7,800 regular tax and CAD 5,200 additional tax. Using CAD 10,000 of assumed eligible deduction leaves CAD 16,000 exposed, with CAD 4,800 regular and CAD 3,200 additional tax. These calculations use an invented flat rate; a real return uses applicable income, provincial rules, deductions and credits.

04

Compare spendable cash with retirement assets before future tax

With no qualifying deduction, the example has CAD 32,000 of returned contributions plus CAD 26,000 AIP, less CAD 13,000 of illustrated current tax. That leaves CAD 45,000 subscriber cash. CAD 6,400 of benefits return to government, and CAD 13,000 is current tax.

With the maximum modeled CAD 10,000 deduction, the subscriber directs CAD 10,000 of the AIP to an eligible retirement plan. The remaining AIP is CAD 16,000. After CAD 8,000 of illustrated current tax, subscriber cash is CAD 40,000; the retirement account has CAD 10,000 before future withdrawal tax, and government benefits returned remain CAD 6,400.

Each stacked bar reconciles to the same CAD 64,400 starting balance. The second scenario has CAD 5,000 less modeled cash now and CAD 10,000 more in retirement assets, alongside CAD 5,000 less illustrative current tax. This is a timing and destination comparison. It does not claim that the extra retirement asset is an equivalent permanent tax saving; future RRSP withdrawals and investment outcomes are outside scope.

The CRA can allow withholding to be waived for a direct transfer when deduction capacity is sufficient and the required procedure is followed. Withholding and final tax are separate. This model calculates neither a source deduction nor a refund or tax balance due, and it assumes that any qualifying transfer and deduction occur as specified.

05

Let both deduction limits vary independently

The sensitivity matrix holds the CAD 26,000 AIP constant. Columns change assumed available deduction capacity from zero to CAD 50,000; rows change how much of the AIP lifetime ceiling was already used. If no lifetime relief has been used, room and the AIP amount can bind. Once CAD 40,000 has been used, only CAD 10,000 remains even in the CAD 50,000 capacity column.

At CAD 50,000 of prior qualifying relief, the model shows zero additional AIP-related reduction. A separate tax-year RRSP deduction may still exist, but the model assigns no AIP tax relief to it. Conversely, a large unused AIP ceiling cannot substitute for missing tax-year deduction capacity.

Use the scenario only after matching a promoter’s statement, contribution and benefit history, AIP eligibility and the subscriber’s current deduction records. Keep the annual tax estimate tied to a specific tax year and province of residence. Recheck current CRA rules and plan documents before a real payment.

The adjacent education-withdrawal guides cover student EAPs, contribution refunds, budgets and grant catch-up. This article isolates a different point in the planning sequence: how confirmed remaining balances might reconcile when an RESP closes and a qualifying subscriber receives accumulated income.
